content: Safflower (Carthamus tinctorius L.) is a highly branched, herbaceous annual plant that resembles a thistle. It typically has numerous long, sharp spines on its leaves. The plant grows to a height of 30 to 150 cm and produces globular flower heads (capitula) that commonly display brilliant yellow, orange, or red flowers, which bloom in July. Each branch of the plant usually bears one to five flower heads, with each head containing 15 to 20 seeds. Safflower is equipped with a strong taproot, allowing it to thrive in arid climates. However, it is highly susceptible to frost damage, particularly during the stages of stem elongation and maturity. Traditionally, safflower was cultivated for its seeds, which were used to color and flavor foods, as well as to produce red (carthamin) and yellow dyes. These dyes were especially valuable before the advent of cheaper aniline dyes. Safflower also had applications in traditional medicine. Over the past fifty years, the plant has been primarily grown for the vegetable oil extracted from its seeds. In April 2007, it was reported that genetically modified safflower had been developed to produce insulin. Safflower oil is flavorless and colorless, with nutritional properties similar to sunflower oil. It is predominantly used as a cooking oil, in salad dressings, and for the production of margarine. Additionally, it can be consumed as a nutritional supplement. The International Nomenclature of Cosmetic Ingredients (INCI) designates it as Carthamus tinctorius. Safflower flowers are sometimes used in cooking as a less expensive substitute for saffron, earning them the nickname bastard saffron. Safflower seeds are also commonly used as an alternative to sunflower seeds in bird feeders, as squirrels tend to dislike their taste. There are two main types of safflower that produce different kinds of oil: one is high in monounsaturated fatty acid (oleic acid), and the other is high in polyunsaturated fatty acid (linoleic acid). Currently, the market favors the former type, as it contains lower levels of saturated fats compared to oils like olive oil. Safflower oil is also used in painting as a substitute for linseed oil, particularly with white pigments, as it lacks the yellow tint characteristic of linseed oil. A strain of safflower known as Lana is cultivated in the southwestern United States, particularly in Arizona and New Mexico. Safflower is one of the oldest crops cultivated by humans. Chemical analysis of ancient Egyptian textiles from the Twelfth Dynasty revealed the presence of dyes derived from safflower. Additionally, garlands made from safflower flowers were discovered in the tomb of Pharaoh Tutankhamun. The Greek name for safflower appears frequently in Linear B tablets, where it is distinguished into two types: white safflower, which was measured, and red safflower, which was weighed. This distinction likely refers to the two usable parts of the plant: the pale seeds and the red florets. In the 19th century, safflower was also known as carthamine. Today, safflower is considered a minor crop, with approximately 600,000 tons produced commercially in over sixty countries worldwide. The leading producers are India, the United States, and Mexico, while Ethiopia, Kazakhstan, China, Argentina, and Australia account for most of the remaining production.
